title: Screen Design & Layout (HCI) — Visual Exam Revision
description: Screen design and layout from HCI, animated: basic principles, the five layout tools (grouping, order, decoration, alignment, white space), physical controls, entering information, knowing what to do, presenting information, aesthetics, colour and 3D, localisation, and prototyping.

scenes.title: Basic principles
lines: Why do some screens feel effortless, and others feel like a puzzle?
Screen design starts with three steps. Ask: what is the user doing?
Think: what information do they need, what comparisons, in what order?
Then design. Form follows function.

scenes.title: The 5 layout tools + mnemonic
lines: You have five tools to lay out a screen.
Grouping of items. Order of items. Decoration, like fonts and boxes. Alignment of items. And white space between them.
Remember: Good Order Deserves A Wow. Grouping, Order, Decoration, Alignment, White space.

scenes.title: Grouping and structure
lines: Tool one. Grouping and structure.
The rule is simple: things that are logically together should be physically together.
Here, the order form fields are scattered. Group them into customer details, address, and payment, and the structure becomes obvious.

scenes.title: Order of groups and items
lines: Tool two. Order. Think: what is the natural order?
The screen order should match it. Use boxes and space to show it, and set the keyboard tab order right.
For instructions, beware the cake recipe syndrome.
Mix milk and flour, add the fruit, after beating them. By the time you read after beating them, it is too late!
Write steps in the order they are done.

scenes.title: Decoration
lines: Tool three. Decoration.
Use boxes to group logical items. Use fonts for emphasis and headings.
But not too many! Five fonts and four colours just create noise.

scenes.title: Alignment: text and names
lines: Tool four. Alignment. In English, we read from left to right, so align text on the left-hand side.
Centered lists look fancy, and are fine for special effects, but they are hard to scan. Left aligned is boring, but readable.
For names, people usually scan for surnames. So make it easy: align the surnames, or put the surname first.

scenes.title: Alignment: numbers
lines: Numbers. Think about the purpose. Which of these is biggest?
Left aligned, you have to read every digit.
Visually, a long number should mean a big number. So align the decimal points, or right align integers.
Now the biggest number jumps out instantly.

scenes.title: Multiple columns
lines: Multiple columns. Scanning across a big gap is hard, and often hard to avoid with database fields.
Fix one: use leaders, a row of dots that carries your eye across.
Fix two: grey alternate rows, so each row stays together.
Fix three, with care: deliberately bad alignment. Right align the labels, so they sit next to their numbers.

scenes.title: White space
lines: Tool five. White space. Look at the letters. The empty space inside them is called the counter.
What you see is shaped as much by the space as by the ink.
White space has three jobs. Space to separate. Space to structure. And space to highlight.

scenes.title: Physical controls: the microwave
lines: These five tools work on physical controls too. Take a microwave.
Grouping: defrost settings, type of food, and time to cook each get their own group.
Order: type of heating, then temperature, then time to cook, then start. The order you actually use it.
Decoration: different colours for different functions, and lines around related buttons.
Alignment: is centered text in buttons easy to scan? And white space: gaps between groups aid grouping.

scenes.title: Entering information
lines: Next, user action and control. First, entering information, in forms and dialogue boxes.
The same layout issues apply. Watch alignment, because labels have different lengths.
Use task analysis for a logical layout and groupings.
Follow the natural order for entering information: top to bottom, left to right, depending on culture. And set the tab order for keyboard entry.

scenes.title: Knowing what to do
lines: Second, knowing what to do. What is active, and what is passive? Where do you click? Where do you type?
A consistent style helps. For example, underlined links on the web.
Use clear labels and icons, and standards for common actions.
Be careful with language. Does bold mean the current state, or the action you can take?
And use affordances: things should look like what they do.

scenes.title: Presenting information
lines: Now, appropriate appearance. Presenting information. Purpose matters.
Choose the sort order: which column, numeric or alphabetic. Choose text or a diagram, a scatter graph or a histogram.
Use paper presentation principles, but add interactivity. Letting users re-order columns softens design choices.

scenes.title: Aesthetics, colour and 3D
lines: Aesthetics and utility. Aesthetically pleasing designs increase user satisfaction and improve productivity.
But beauty and utility may conflict. A pretty background behind text is good to look at, but hard to read.
Colour and three D are both often used very badly. Use colour sparingly, to reinforce other information. And beware colour blindness.
Test: turn your monitor to greys only. Can you still read your screen?
Three D is good for physical information, but text in perspective and three D pie charts? No.

scenes.title: Localisation and internationalisation
lines: Across countries and cultures: localisation and internationalisation, changing interfaces for particular cultures and languages.
Globalisation means choosing symbols that work everywhere.
Simply changing the language? Use a resource database instead of literal text. But translations change sizes, and even left-right order.
There are deeper issues too: cultural values, and the meaning of symbols. A tick and a cross mean yes and no in some cultures, but both just mean mark this in others.

scenes.title: Iteration and prototyping
lines: Finally, prototyping. You never get it right first time. If at first you don't succeed, iterate.
But beware. Moving little by little, where are you heading? The Malvern hills, or the Matterhorn?
Small improvements can trap you on a small hill. So you need a good start point, and you need to understand what is wrong.

scenes.title: Recap
lines: Recap. Ask, think, design. Form follows function.
Five tools: Good Order Deserves A Wow. Grouping, order, decoration, alignment, white space.
Then user action: entering info, knowing what to do, and affordances.
Appearance: presenting info, aesthetics, colour and three D, and culture. And always, iterate with prototypes.
